title: Blind guides (Luke 6:39–49)
hookLine: a good person out of the good treasure of the heart brings good
carry: out of the heart the mouth speaks

lines: CAN THE BLIND LEAD THE BLIND?
A DITCH, A SPECK, A TREE, A HOUSE.
cards: "Can the blind lead the blind? shall they not both fall into the ditch?" Jesus says it almost like a riddle, the kind of saying you'd hear at a village well.

It's the last stretch of the sermon on the plain, and the tone changes. After love your enemies and the heaped measure, he turns to the people who guide others: parents, teachers, bosses, friends who give advice.
Which is everyone. And he offers quick pictures, one after another: a ditch, a speck of dust, a fig tree, a storehouse, a house in a flood.

teach.b: First, the speck: "And why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother's eye, but perceivest not the beam that is in thine own eye?" A mote is a speck of dust. A beam is a wooden roof beam.
The picture is meant to be funny: a man with a plank sticking out of his face, squinting at his friend's eyelash. Fix your own sight first.
Second, the tree: "For of thorns men do not gather figs, nor of a bramble bush gather they grapes." You judge a tree by what grows on it.

Third, the heart: "A good man out of the good treasure of his heart bringeth forth that which is good; and an evil man out of the evil treasure of his heart bringeth forth that which is evil: for of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaketh."
Treasure here is thesauros, a storehouse. Whatever you've been storing comes out when you open your mouth.

teach.h: A TREE IS KNOWN BY ITS FRUIT.
teach.b: Words are the fruit; the heart is the tree.
Someone who hears and does is like a man who "digged deep, and laid the foundation on a rock." The flood comes, and the house stands.

teach.h: OF THE ABUNDANCE OF THE HEART HIS MOUTH SPEAKETH.
teach.b: Someone who hears and doesn't do built on bare earth, and the flood takes it. So the blind guide isn't someone without sight. It's someone who hasn't looked inward, who talks without doing.

how: Christians often quote the mote and the beam as a check before judging others, and the house built on the rock is a familiar Sunday school song and sermon picture.

o: those who guide others without looking inward
leaders who can't see what's coming next
teachers who refuse to listen to questions

games.q: what's inside Luke 6:39–49 — tap the pairs.

s: the mote and the beam is meant to be a little funny
a man with a plank in his eye squinting at a speck in his friend's.
Luke's wise builder simply built on a rock
Luke says he digged deep and laid the foundation on a rock.
thesauros means a storehouse, where you keep things.

games.q: you notice a speck in your friend's eye and want to help. what does Jesus say to do first?
o: take the beam out of your own eye.
games.why: first cast out the beam from your own eye; then you'll see clearly to help with your friend's speck.

practice: Picture your heart as a storehouse, shelves and barrels, and look honestly at what's been stored this week: worry, gratitude, a grudge, a kind thing someone said.
Then find something good on those shelves, a memory of kindness or something that made you laugh, and hold it for a few breaths.
If you pray, you can ask for a good storehouse; if you don't, simply rest with the good thing you found.

wordCard.voice: Blind guides. Jesus' warning about guiding others without looking inward first, and his picture of words coming out of the storehouse of the heart.

orig.note: Greek: a treasure, or the storehouse where treasure is kept. English gets thesaurus from it.

carryVoice: Your line: out of the heart the mouth speaks. A week of a tearing net, a hole in a roof, new wine, a night of prayer, the plain, a heaped measure and a storehouse. Day five hundred twenty-five, and another week on the path.
